summary:
NASA has explored Mars for decades with robots and missions that have collected data about its surface, climate, minerals, and environment. Astronauts will need detailed maps, but current maps are general and regional, not made for planning specific routes. Because explorers will have limited oxygen, they must understand terrain risks and know how long they can walk without endangering their return.

BreathPath helps astronauts plan safe walks on Mars. It calculates routes considering available oxygen time, terrain slopes, dust, and communication problems. Its main feature, the Return Horizon, shows how far an astronaut can go and still return safely using the rule of thirds. Astronauts activate five data layers, set their maximum slope, and enter their suit’s oxygen; BreathPath then updates the safe route and identifies shelters. It works on a tablet or helmet display.

The project uses NASA data: MOLA and HiRISE (terrain), THEMIS (thermal), CRISM (minerals), MEDA (weather), RAD (radiation), and Mars Trek (JPL). The prototype’s layers are synthetic. It was built with Python, JavaScript, HTML, and Dijkstra’s algorithm, with Claude AI supporting code, text, and slides, reviewed by the team.

Next steps: real Jezero data, live MEDA weather, a team mode, and a helmet display version. BreathPath turns Mars data into decisions that protect astronauts, answering one question before every exploration: can I reach that location and return safely?
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
BreathPath is an interactive, hyper-local map of Jezero crater that helps astronauts plan safe walks on Mars. It measures every step in oxygen-minutes instead of kilometers. Each map cell has a cost that slope, dust and weak communications raise, and cells steeper than the limit are blocked. Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the lowest-cost route from the base to the science target. A second search measures the oxygen needed to reach each cell and draws the Return Horizon using the rule of thirds: ⅓ of the oxygen to go out, ⅓ to come back and ⅓ in reserve. The astronaut toggles five layers (relief, slope, dust, communications and Return Horizon), sets a maximum slope and the suit’s oxygen, and the route and shelters update instantly.

What are its benefits?
It helps a crew plan a walk that is safer, faster and more useful for science. It makes the consumables budget visible on the map. It also leaves an open, simple model that can load real elevation data.

What is the expected impact?
It turns Mars data into one decision before every outing: can I get there and still get back? This lowers the risk of future human missions and shows how technology and scientific data can make space exploration easier. The next steps are the real Jezero elevation model, live MEDA weather, a buddy-pair mode and a helmet display.

What tools, programming languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Python with NumPy, Pillow and python-pptx for the route model, map images and slides.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the demo page.
  • Dijkstra’s algorithm (1959) for route finding.
  • Claude (Anthropic) as our AI assistant and main reference. It helped with research, the route model, code, text, slides and translation. The team reviewed and decided all the content.
  • Microsoft PowerPoint for the presentation, Google Drive for sharing files and Google Sites for the web page.
  • NASA data that inspired the project: MOLA and HiRISE (relief), THEMIS (thermal), CRISM (minerals), MEDA (weather), RAD (radiation) and Mars Trek (JPL). The prototype layers are synthetic, shaped like Jezero, and are not real measurements.
  • Hardware: the team’s computers, using their own internet connection and the AT&T mobile network. The final design is meant for a tablet or a helmet display.

How is it creative?

  • Oxygen-minutes map: the best route is the one that uses the least air, not the shortest one.
  • Return Horizon: a live boundary that darkens places from which the astronaut could no longer get back.
  • Escape-first logic: if a science target fails the rule of thirds, the map rejects it and points to the nearest shelter.
  • Live alerts: a dust storm alert raises the dust cost and recalculates the route.
  • Bilingual: it works in English and Spanish.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Safety first: a conservative rule of thirds and shelters always in view.
  • Real conditions on Mars: limited oxygen, slope, dust, weak communications and distant help.
  • Scientific honesty: we state clearly that the layers are synthetic and that the thresholds are team design choices, not NASA rules.
  • Responsible use of AI: we say where Claude helped and we reviewed all the content.
  • Practical use: a simple interface for a tablet or helmet.
  • Respect for NASA: we used no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
